Energy E^tot can be unbounded below when W has negative eigenvalues and Ω does not compensate. This well-posedness issue is not addressed by the paper.
When E^tot is unbounded below, the 'gradient flow' does not converge to a minimizer: ||F|| diverges and the energy-dissipation argument becomes vacuous because E → -∞.
Describing the evolution equations as following steepest descent of a learnable energy is misleading if that energy is unbounded below.
The paper should discuss constraining Ω (e.g., Ω ⪰ W in Loewner order) so that E^tot is guaranteed bounded below and the gradient flow is well-posed.
The HFD claim requires ρ_- to dominate: |λ_-^W|(ρ_Δ−1) > λ_+^W. Since ρ_Δ−1 ≤ 1, this demands more mass on negative eigenvalues of W; the condition needs explicit treatment.

Section 4's claim that high-frequency dominance via negative W eigenvalues is impossible without the residual connection extends prior analyses (Oono & Suzuki; Cai & Wang), which should be acknowledged.
The Euler discretization F_{k+1}=F_k+εĀF_kW−εF_kΩ corresponds to a residual GNN; what happens when the residual connection is dropped is left unresolved and needs clarification.
Assumption 4.2's claimed equivalence between increasing average expected rewards and decreasing d_t is mathematically false; a counterexample can make d_t increase while average reward increases.
The paper claims dependence on true d_T rather than max, but if d_t is increasing then d_T equals the max, so the bound still relies on max.
Assumption 4.2 requires i-star's cumulative expected reward to dominate every other learner for all t, implying a higher first reward and not generally guaranteed in RL.
The assumption that i-star monotonically dominates every other learner is very strong and may not hold in practice.
Because the equivalence to decreasing d_t is false and the domination assumption is strong, the theoretical regret guarantees are questionable.
Event E confidence interval in Eq (3) is ambiguous: if u_t is an expected sum over n_t plays, the sqrt n_t scaling needs checking; if it is an average, the interval form differs.
The Lemma bound using d_T sqrt n_T should be checked for consistency with the sum-based confidence interval.

Claim of 'first time' is strong and likely false; prior work such as Segmenter, MaskFormer/Mask2Former, and SETR already use attention or similarity for segmentation. Suggest tempering the novelty claim.
ATM may be novel in using sigmoid on the similarity map as a mask, but the 'for first time' phrasing overclaims; recommend softening.

Sigmoid(S) yields per-class masks independently without cross-class normalization; final output multiplies class probabilities by masks, with focal/dice mask loss per class. This is similar to MaskFormer.
MaskFormer already generates masks via dot product between query embeddings and pixel embeddings. ATM can be seen as removing the MLP and using attention QK, so its novelty is questionable.
Using one class token per class differs from MaskFormer's multiple non-class-specific queries. This may limit mask-generation capacity and flexibility, especially for classes with multiple modes.
How does one token per class capture multiple modes or intra-class variation? Multi-layer ATM refines masks, but one query per class may underperform on ambiguous classes.

Multi-head attention details are unclear: do you sum similarity maps across heads before sigmoid? Summing raw logits changes scale versus standard per-head softmax and averaging/concatenation. Clarify Eq (2).

The dynamics may diverge rather than converge to a minimizer; treating it as gradient flow of a learnable energy is questionable.
For HFD, F(t)/||F(t)|| converges to a high-frequency eigenvector, but the norm may grow exponentially.
If the energy is unbounded below, it decreases indefinitely, so there is no minimizer; this conflicts with the usual gradient flow picture where energy dissipates.
It is unclear whether Ω or the external term (Ω - W) can stabilize the negative Dirichlet term.
The negative Dirichlet term is unbounded because edge gradients can be arbitrarily large.
The external quadratic term may offset negative Dirichlet if Ω-W is positive definite, but scaling a high-frequency eigenvector makes both terms quadratic; boundedness depends on the coefficient.
If Ω-W has smallest eigenvalue > ρΔ, energy may be bounded below; otherwise negative Dirichlet can dominate and make energy unbounded below.
The HFD regime may intentionally drive energy to -∞ as the norm grows, representing repulsion sharpening.
Gradient flow of an unbounded energy may lack global existence; solutions may blow up in finite time.
For Ω=0, linear ODE analysis via diagonalizing A and W shows components grow when A has negative high-frequency eigenvalues and W has negative eigenvalues, explaining HFD norm growth.
This raises a conceptual issue: lack of minimizers and non-standard over-smoothing analysis.
Definition 2.1 of smoothing is odd/weak: E^Dir ≤ C + φ(t) with C depending only on initial and φdot ≤0 is satisfied by any bounded energy with C=initial.
Defining over-smoothing as E→0 or E_L→0 is acceptable.
Definition 2.2 L/HFD: E^Dir(F/||F||) → 0 (or ρΔ/2). For normalized F, E^Dir ≤ ρΔ/2 because max eigenvalue of I_d⊗Δ is ρΔ.

Eq (2) correctly specifies the Plackett-Luce likelihood: product over k=1..K, denominator sum_{i=k}^K; the k=K term is 1, so loss covers K-1 choices.

If f is average, ranking depends on mean reward because C is common; if f is soft max, e_phi is log-sum-exp, acceptable for ranking.
Reward is bounded [0,1], but Plackett-Luce uses exp(e_phi). For long sequences e_phi can be as large as T, so softmax differences may saturate and cause vanishing gradients.

C in Eq (3) is average length, so multiplying by C changes the softmax temperature. Since C depends on the group's average length, effective temperature varies across groups, which may be undesirable.
Soft max/min are not length-invariant. With the C factor, log-sum-exp grows like log T for long sequences, reintroducing length bias even if per-token rewards are equal.
For e^max ≈ C(μ + β log T), C grows with average length, so within a group longer sequences get higher scores even when max token reward is the same.
This contradicts the stated goal of mitigating length bias. Soft max was presented as an alternative to summation, but the C factor may reintroduce length dependence.
Finite β leaves a β log T length term. If β→0 the bias vanishes, but they use finite β and do not discuss how to tune it or its impact.
Soft minimum suffers the same length-bias issue as soft maximum when multiplied by C.
For average aggregation, e^avg = C * mean_r. If mean reward is independent of length, there is no length bias except the common C multiplier.
They discard neutral data: SFT uses only positive feedback, while RL downweights negative feedback, limiting available learning signals.
Positive feedback often confirms already correct actions; training on positives may reinforce correct actions but may not teach new correct actions, and exploration may be insufficient.
Need mechanism analysis and ablations to determine whether the model learns from corrections (negative feedback) or positive reinforcement, and which system variant works best.
The prompt instruction 'Lean towards negative if it sounds neutral' may cause conservative negative bias; with negative reward -0.1, sensitivity analysis is needed.
The prompt lists 'simply move on to the next stage' as positive, but this can be neutral and may cause feedback misclassification.
If an action contains multiple image selections/deselections, follow-up feedback may refer only to a subset; assigning one label to the whole action is coarse and needs discussion.
Categorical feedback may be unavailable for the final turn when the interaction ends; the label is unspecified, potentially biasing toward actions with follow-ups.
For successful interactions, the last action may have no follow-up utterance; how to decode feedback for the final action is unspecified.

The paper text ends mid-sentence in §3, so no experimental tables, numbers, or supplemental material are available; the review focuses on the method and claims and flags where empirical verification is required.
Mining a procedural prior directly from video demonstrations, rather than reusing a WikiHow-style script, is a clean, well-motivated reframing of an under-exploited signal.
The argument in §3 that video reveals which transitions are common and how strong each dependency is, versus a rigid script, is well articulated.
The contrast with the DTW family, which is monotonic and must place everything, and with independent per-clip classification is crisp.
The Fig. 3 illustration, showing directional edges, top-k next keysteps, and cross-task sharing, is compelling if the underlying statistics hold.

The graph formulation is simple and interpretable: defining edge weight as normalized empirical transition count and using negative-log plus Dijkstra is technically straightforward and scales conceptually to large vocabularies.
The keep-confident, repair-unconfident design is a sensible and easily reusable recipe.
The evaluation targets are broad, aiming at both keystep recognition and localization and at large-scale video representation learning, with multiple downstream tasks.
If the numbers hold up, this would be a materially stronger contribution than a gain on a single benchmark.
The core inference step of assigning the mined path to clips is under-specified and appears technically unsound.

Length mismatch is unaddressed: if the max-probability path has N keysteps and the interval spans M clips, it is unclear what happens for M much greater than N or M much less than N; this is common in long-gap HowTo100M cases.
Uniform mapping of the path discards clip-level similarity scores that indicated a clip was merely low confidence rather than uninformative.
They claim sum of k_i equals 1, but this is false due to the last clip and absences; this may be an issue.
Directionality claim may be trivial: pairs are directional only because of temporal order in noisy preliminary labels, not validated true relations.
No validation that graph edges/directionality reflect true structure rather than noise from preliminary labels.
PathSearch uses negative log probabilities; zero-probability transitions yield infinite cost and no path. Smoothing/backoff is needed but not mentioned.
With K=10,588 and many unseen pairs, graph is sparse; anchors may be disconnected, so path search fails. Handling disconnected nodes is not discussed.
Uniform assignment of path keysteps between anchors ignores the actual number of video segments and intermediate confidence scores.
Uniform assignment is ill-defined when path keysteps mismatch segment count: unclear which keysteps to merge/drop; needs clarification and evaluation.
They call it a beam-search approach but use Dijkstra; beam search is not Dijkstra, so terminology is inconsistent.
No probabilistic calibration of confidence scores is provided.
The threshold gamma is global; sensitivity analysis is needed because too high/low values change graph usage.
Zero-shot claim is questionable if graph is mined from unlabeled videos of the same target dataset (transductive), not transferred from HowTo100M; need clarification.
The similarity function in Eq. (2) is not normalized to [0,1]; this should be clarified or justified.
The loss is not a correct/standard contrastive loss; its formulation and relation to InfoNCE need precise definition.
The negative set D- includes both random and neighbor negatives, but the loss sums over all pairs equally without distinguishing them.

With multiple negatives per positive, the loss treats each negative independently rather than using a softmax over one positive and K negatives as in standard InfoNCE; if it is binary classification, state so.
Fine-tuning details are missing; Section 3.4 is referenced but not described in the provided text, so the fine-tuning protocol is unclear.
The provided manuscript is truncated after Eq. 4 and lacks experimental results, making it impossible to verify the paper's claims.

The method requires the density ratio d^E/d^D (or d^D/d^E), which is generally unavailable; the paper does not specify how to estimate it, and empirical counts/KDE in continuous settings would be high variance.

Parameterization of the upper-level reward correction Δr(s,a,~r) is unspecified; with continuous reward a neural network may be high-dimensional, and learning Δr(s,a,0) when rewards are zero is unclear.

The two-timescale first-order bilevel optimization appears to ignore implicit differentiation through the lower-level V*, which can bias upper-level updates unless V converges before each update; convergence is not proven in the main text.

Policy extraction is not detailed: computing π(a|s) from g requires estimating d^D(s,a) and normalizing over actions, especially in continuous action spaces; weighted behavior cloning is only implied.
The D4RL experimental setup is absent from the provided text, so the claim of superior performance cannot be verified.
It is unclear how imperfect rewards are generated and how expert data are obtained; D4RL datasets already contain rewards, and whether a small expert subset is used is not stated.
Baselines, whether they receive the same expert data, and comparison protocols are not described.
Ablations and compute costs are not reported, leaving the empirical contribution difficult to assess.
Statistical significance and hyperparameter sensitivity are not reported, so the robustness of the results is unclear.
The paper lacks convergence or performance guarantees for the proposed bilevel optimization.
There is no proof that RGM recovers the optimal policy with perfect rewards; the upper-level correction may still alter rewards because Δr lacks regularization constraints.
Because Δr is unconstrained, f-divergence minimization can make the policy match the expert exactly and override even correct reward signals, so preservation of useful information is not guaranteed.
With limited expert data, d^E has sparse support; minimizing f-divergence to it may encourage pure imitation of expert states/actions and ignore reward learning.
The method may be non-identifiable and overfit the expert data due to lack of regularization on Δr.
The f-divergence choice and its estimation are not specified.
How many expert trajectories are used and how small the expert dataset is remain unclear.
FDE consistently underestimates similarity: when q's cluster disagrees with the true nearest p in multiple bits, fill_emptyClusters selects a less-similar p, so q's contribution is a lower bound.
The quality bound requires LSH to guarantee the nearest p is in the same cluster, or in a cluster with very few disagreeing bits; otherwise the guarantee fails.
The 'strictly faster than brute-force' claim is incomplete: if d_FDE is large, the MIPS stage itself is expensive; the comparison omits this cost.
The theoretical FDE dimension (m/delta)^{O(1/epsilon)} is astronomically large for epsilon ~0.1, e.g. about 10^30, making the theoretical guarantee essentially vacuous.
Theory-practice mismatch: Theorem 2.1's huge dimension conflicts with the abstract's 10,240-dimensional FDEs, so the theory does not match practical dimensions.
The authors should explicitly acknowledge the gap between theory and practice rather than presenting the theoretical guarantee without caveat.
The 'data-oblivious' claim is loose: k-means centers and fill_emptyClusters use data, and document FDEs depend on the document set P.
Comparison to PLAID/ColBERT is unfair: MUVERA scans the full dataset in MIPS while PLAID prunes; fair comparison needs equal-latency or recall-vs-latency curves.
The claimed 90% lower latency may reflect PLAID reproduction or implementation issues rather than algorithmic superiority; this needs verification.
Notation is inconsistent: P is used for a document and D for the dataset, with Q,P subset R^d; this is confusing.
Chamfer similarity sign is unclear: inner products of normalized embeddings can be negative, so normalized Chamfer lies between -1 and 1.
Asymmetric query and document FDE norms may affect MIPS solvers and pruning or coarse quantization quality, though this is not critical.
Product Quantization compression may be problematic: PQ assumes uniformly distributed coordinates across subspaces, but FDEs may have structural zeros or sparsity.
Evaluation and comparisons in the experiments section cannot be assessed because that section is missing or truncated in the review copy.
The claim that DESSERT runs no faster than brute force in the worst case is questionable or unsupported and needs justification.
The nearest p to a cone can be far from q if no p lies in that cone, undermining the assumption that fill_empty recovers a close point.
If k is large, clusters are small, so a close p and q may not fall in the same cluster.
fill_empty selects p with fewest disagreeing hash bits; for SimHash this only roughly corresponds to angular distance.
With large k, the closest p in hash space may still be far from q.
The theorem may require a different LSH family, but SimHash is only for angular distance.
Using k_sim bits to create B=2^k clusters is AND amplification, without the usual OR amplification.
Increasing k reduces false positives but also reduces true positives, creating a bias-variance tension.
fill_emptyClusters cannot correct errors when the close point falls in a different non-empty cluster.
If q's cluster contains another point p', that far point may contribute instead of the true close p.
To avoid error, q's cluster must be empty of other points or contain p.
The expected number of separating hyperplanes is kθ/π; for θ~sqrt(ε), this is large, so p is not closest in hash space.
Many other points could have fewer disagreeing bits, so fill_empty may pick a far point and the theory seems suspicious.
If ε is small, distinguishing inner-product differences near ε requires many bits, but ensuring the optimal point collides requires few bits.
There is a fundamental tension: a single hash cannot guarantee both close-point collision and far-point separation.
Standard ANN LSH uses multiple tables (OR amplification) plus AND amplification; here R_reps=1 leaves only one table.
The analysis assumes k_sim = O(log(mδ^{-1})/ε); for large ε k is small, for small ε k is large.
The paper's theory is confusing and may over-commit before resolving these LSH guarantees.

The proof's handling of classifiers with more than two classes is valid: one can pick a label y* with volume fraction ≤1/2, and any z classified differently from y* is misclassified since y* is the true label.
The no-abstain assumption ensures the sum of volumes over labels equals vol(B), so a label with volume ≤1/2 can always be chosen when there are at least two classes.

If the classifier's label set includes labels not in Y, picking y* from Y remains acceptable; if all Y labels have volume >1/2 it is impossible, and if their total volume is <1/2, non-Y classifications count as misclassifications.
If the classifier has only one class, its volume fraction is 1, not ≤1/2, so the requirement of two or more classes is necessary and fine.

The proof's claim that for every class y, at least 1-δ mass of examples lies within distance rδ of the origin is acceptable even for unbounded support; rδ exists but may be huge, and R = rδ sqrt(n2)/δ is fine.

The claim that moving a ball of radius R by distance rδ keeps at least 1-δ of the new ball's volume inside the old ball is initially questionable and needs high-dimensional concentration verification.

For two balls radius R at distance d=rδ, the outside volume is a small spherical cap; with d/R = δ/sqrt(n2), the cap fraction is exponentially small, so the intersection claim holds and the constant is fine.
Further checking R = rδ sqrt(n2)/δ gives d/R = δ/sqrt(n2); for large n2 the cap fraction is negligible, confirming the proof's constant.
Theorem 4.1 states that with probability at least 1/2 - δ for some δ0 > 0, F(x)+δ0 v is not labeled y*; the proof picks z_x uniformly in B_x and sets v = (z_x - x)/||z_x - x||_2.
The proof's step defining v as (z_x - x)/||z_x - x||_2 from a uniform z_x in B_x raises a question: is this v uniform on the sphere? The text cuts off before resolving it.

The paper overclaims being first to provably show the power of 'don't know' in adversarially robust classifier design, ignoring prior conformal prediction, selective classification, and abstention work.
Theorem 4.1 claims all classifiers without abstention are vulnerable, but the proof appears to have gaps.
The definition of the adversary in Theorem 4.1 is unclear.

The theorem's guarantee is very weak and essentially reduces to the trivial observation that no classifier is robust in all classes; a classifier can be perfect on one class and vulnerable on the other.
The small-perturbation result, where δ0 depends on x and a random perturbation flips classification, resembles the known high-dimensional phenomenon that decision boundaries are everywhere.
In the proof, if the decision boundary is far from the origin, the theorem is satisfied trivially because almost all of the ball can belong to one class.

The ball argument is problematic: if all of B is class 0, choosing y*=1 and perturbing near the origin does not imply misclassification; the proof may conflate being classified differently from y* with an actual error.
The perturbation success probability ≥1/2−δ and arbitrarily small δ0 are used, but δ0 depends on x, weakening the adversarial guarantee.
The manuscript as provided ends mid-sentence of Lemma 2; the proof of Theorem 2 is missing, so Theorem 2 cannot be verified.
The max+min identity used for MAM neurons holds only when at least one input value is zero; otherwise max(a,0)+min(a,0) does not equal a.
Lemma 1 sets other input weights to zero so a zero is present, but this relies on N>1; the paper assumes N>1 without stating it in the theorem.
For N=1, a MAM neuron with one input computes max(v)+min(v)=2v, not v, so it is not equivalent to a MAC neuron.
The theorem does not explicitly restrict N>1; to make the construction valid for N=1, the architecture needs a dummy constant or zero-weight input, or an explicit N>=2 assumption.
Setting other input weights to zero in Lemma 1 still adds parameters; this is acceptable under arbitrary width but should be noted.
In the second hidden layer, zero weights on other first-hidden neurons are needed to include 0 in the max; for N>1 there are enough such neurons.
For N=1, the pair y_i^L and y_i^R guarantees one is zero at any x, so max over -y^L and -y^R already includes 0; the extra zero term may not be necessary.
Formula (8) writes max over {0, -y_i^L, -y_i^R}; this 0 must correspond to an actual zero input or bias, but bias is added after max+min, so the notation is ambiguous.
If x lies in [omega_i-l, omega_i+l], both y_i^L and y_i^R are zero; outside, one is positive and the other zero, so max includes 0.
For N>1, each pair also contributes a zero, so the zero term in max may be justified, but this is not made explicit.
